Local Arizona history — Yuma Territorial Prison (1825), its rock-cut 'cave' cells and manacle rings, now a museum — decodes the old man's ravings about caves, ovens and filth.
The threatening old man is not malevolent but a tormented soul, imprisoned and baked in stone cells, whose violence stems from terror of being returned and an unappeasable thirst.

Art forgery and theft: a museum restorer copies a Delgardi madonna, swaps his forgery for the original on display, then claims to have 'discovered' the original beneath his own Albretti canvas. Central question: which painting will the experts declare genuine?

The museum's restoring and retouching section and old-masters gallery, plus Widner's skylit studio apartment — a small insider world where only a keyholding staff restorer could access and swap the painting
Carl Widner, the 64-year-old head of restoration, narrating his own crime; motive is money for retirement on the Riviera plus revenge on the critics who dismissed his art
The museum (its trustees and its half-million-dollar Delgardi acquisition), targeted because the board's sudden mandatory retirement rule left Widner destitute; also the critics who scorned him

Ironic reversal rather than detection: X-rays, alcohol tests and spectroscopic analysis lead the experts to unanimously certify Widner's forgery as genuine, reasoning his deliberate cobalt-blue 'flaw' proves 150-year-old retouching; he keeps no money but gains the secret triumph of his work hanging as a masterpiece
First-person culprit-narrator: Carl Widner, eccentric elderly restorer; the nominal investigators are the curator and the panel of art experts

Effectively no suspect cast — inverted narrative told by the perpetrator, Carl Widner, museum restorer. The only other figures (assistant Henry Sansom, the curator, the board, the panel of experts) function as authorities/dupes rather than suspects; no one is ever suspected at all.

The two deliberate spots of cobalt blue Widner paints into his forgery as a 'giveaway' anachronism — planted misdirection that ironically backfires, being read by the experts as proof of 19th-century retouching and thus of the painting's age.

Fully fair-play in the inverted mode: the reader is given the entire forgery technique in advance — support/ground/paint/varnish layers, pigment dating (Prussian blue 1704, cobalt 1802, synthetic ultramarine 1824), badger-hair brushes, oven-baked craquelure and scraped grime — so the experts' reasoning can be tested by the reader.

Technical authentication reversed: X rays, alcohol tests and spectroscopic analyses, plus the anachronistic cobalt-blue pigment, are used by the experts to certify the forgery as genuine and the original as a student copy — the demonstration lands on the forger himself via the curator's phone call.

Institutional art-world hierarchy: museum trustees who impose mandatory retirement at 65, a curator and chairman above the restoring-and-retouching section head, and critics whose verdicts define artistic worth. Authenticity is decided by credentialed experts with half a million dollars of institutional money at stake.

No alibi in the conventional sense; Widner's cover story is legitimate access — he holds a museum key for weekend work and turns off the alarms, then frames his possession of the second painting as an innocent restoration 'discovery'.

Widner (perpetrator-narrator, the story's de facto investigator of expertise) is wounded by critical rejection and forced retirement — a sixty-four-year-old artist whose work has never been called original, driven by poverty and the craving to be validated; the case exploits exactly that vanity, and the 'defeat' becomes his consolation.

The 'victim' is institutional — the museum. Widner's grievance web runs against the trustees who abruptly invoked mandatory retirement at sixty-five after a century of laissez-faire, and against the art critics who have publicly savaged work he never asked them to judge.

The museum's closed hours, alarm systems and keyed access define the only possible substitution window — and Widner, as a section head who 'often worked weekends,' held the key and the alarm codes, so the very security that should have limited him was his instrument.

Widner himself is the only plausible suspect and his vulnerabilities are exactly what the crime activates: near-bankruptcy ($900 and a car), impending forced retirement, eccentric reputation, museum keys, and a fifteen-year career in retouching that gives him the skill. Yet nobody suspects him — because his wound (vanity as a failed painter) makes him volunteer his own 'discovery.'

Albretti, the long-dead minor Renaissance student of Delgardi, is retroactively cast as the 'copyist' — the experts attribute Widner's forgery to him, so a centuries-dead painter absorbs the blame that should have exposed the crime.

The entire story is told by the forger himself, a self-flattering first-person narrator who insists he is a 'young sixty-four,' dismisses critics as dastardly, and re-frames total failure as triumph in the final lines. His self-assessment of his talent, and his final claim that fame beats money, cannot be trusted.

The forger's craft as codified by van Meegeren: a painting's four layers (support, ground, paint, varnish); the impossibility of faking old canvas so an authentic period painting must be stripped and reused; period-correct pigment chronology (ultramarine, Prussian blue 1704, cobalt 1802, synthetic ultramarine 1824); badger-hair rather than hog-bristle brushes; varnish, oven-baking to craquelure, and dusting with authentic scraped grime.

Widner is a genuinely skilled craftsman pushed out by an arbitrary retirement rule into penury, humiliated by critics whose opinions he never solicited; his theft is as much a bid for artistic vindication as for money — and he ends by renouncing the money, content that his own work hangs admired as a master's. The experts' complicity (half a million invested in the wall) makes the institution look no cleaner than he is.
Bludgeoning murder of a housewife with a lead pipe in her kitchen, staged as a burglary; central question: was it a burglar or the husband, and can his alibi be broken?
A cramped block of tiny brick bungalows on midget lots, with the crime confined to the narrow time window between 9:00 and 10:50 a.m.
Joseph Eldridge, the husband, killed his wife for her savings and to be with his mistress-neighbor Mimi Jenks, who supplied a false alibi in exchange for promised marriage and Caribbean luxury
May Eldridge, 33-year-old schoolteacher wife whose ten years of unspent teaching salary made her worth more dead than divorced to her husband
Galton stages a sting: a pretty policewoman poses as another woman alibiing Eldridge, and jealousy makes Mrs. Jenks recant, confess the false alibi and reveal the bloody shirt and jewelry box
Captain of Detectives Mike Galton, veteran official 'old man' with institutional authority, aided by Detective Dennis and his policewoman daughter Jenny

Very small cast: the husband Joseph Eldridge (motive: wife's ten years of unspent teaching salary; opportunity: alone in house before shopping trip), a hypothetical anonymous burglar, and the neighbor Mimi Jenks, a divorced 'grass widow' who appears only as a witness/alibi but proves to be the accomplice-lover.
The staged burglary — ransacked bureaus, missing jewelry box and cash from the purse, and the untraceable length of lead pipe brought from outside — designed to suggest an intruder killed her.

Fair: the reader sees everything Galton sees — Mrs. Jenks's shorts, halter and bleached hair, her alimony status, the wife working all week while the husband is a free-lance agent at home, and the unspent teaching salary — all stated before the solution.

A psychological sting: Galton dresses his pretty daughter Jenny as 'Miss Murphy,' a supposed second alibi witness and rival lover; jealousy makes Mrs. Jenks break, recant the alibi, and reveal the bloody shirt wrapped around the jewelry box in her laundry bag.

Lower-middle-class suburb of identical brick bungalows; gender-role tension in a marriage where the wife's teacher's salary outstrips the insurance salesman husband; police hierarchy with the 'old man' captain, his junior detective, and his own daughter as policewoman.

Eldridge claims he left to do the Saturday marketing between 8:50 and 9:10 and returned at 10:50, with the checkout clock at 10:40; corroborated only by neighbor Mrs. Jenks who swears his car left at nine. The alibi is false — she is his lover and he actually left at 9:35 after killing his wife and changing his bloody shirt.

May Eldridge had no outside enemies — the grievance web is entirely domestic: her husband Joseph, who wanted her ten years' worth of unspent teaching salary and freedom to run off with the neighbor, and Mimi Jenks, the mistress next door who saw the wife as the obstacle to marriage and Caribbean luxury.

A cramped tract of identical brick bungalows on midget lots — houses so close that a neighbor's open bedroom window is the only witness to a car starting. The proximity that makes the affair possible also makes the mistress the sole alibi witness, and the absence of any other witnesses forces the detective toward a psychological rather than physical solution.

Joseph Eldridge is the only person with opportunity and no one to corroborate his shopping trip; his adultery and financial dependence on his wife's salary make his grief suspect. Mimi Jenks's vulnerability is jealousy — the fear of being 'left holding the bag' while another woman takes him.

The imaginary burglar — the ransacked bureaus, emptied purse, missing rings and jewelry box were staged by Eldridge to suggest a stranger came in the open back door. Briefly, the phantom 'Miss Murphy' also functions as a fabricated rival.

Both Joseph Eldridge and Mimi Jenks give false accounts. Eldridge's timeline (left at nine, returned at ten-fifty) is a fabrication; Mrs. Jenks's eager, over-detailed corroboration ('I looked at the clock... did my exercises by the window for fifteen minutes') is a purchased lie. He actually left at nine-thirty-five after killing his wife and changing a bloodied shirt.

The domain knowledge is applied psychology rather than forensics: Galton's read of human nature — that a sexy young grass widow next door to a handsome insurance man whose wife works all day means an affair, and that a jealous accomplice will destroy an alibi the instant she believes a younger rival is also lying to save him.

Thin but present: Eldridge is a man kept by his wife's salary, emasculated by doing the Saturday marketing while she taught, drawn to the neighbor and to a promised life of Caribbean luxury; Mrs. Jenks is a discarded wife living on alimony checks who traded perjury for a promise of marriage. Galton himself uses his own daughter as sexual bait to entrap a witness.

Double stabbing murder in a future society that has no concept or legal category of murder; the question is not whodunit but whether an unprecedented crime can be detected by a state with no detectives
Complex 55, a walled totalitarian dormitory-work complex of about a hundred thousand members under surveillance by microphones and television screens
Paul 2473, air filtration engineer, who murdered to void the Mating Assignments and obtain Carol 7427, believing the state had no apparatus to punish murder

Richard 3833 (Virus Chemistry worker) and Laura 6356 (calculation machine operator) — killable because they were assigned as mates to Carol 7427 and Paul, blocking Paul's desired pairing; both worked in isolation

The state mass-processes the entire complex with truth-serum injections; Paul confesses under the drug, is tried publicly, and is tortured in a glass cage as a traitor guilty of destroying state property
No detective; the lens is the murderer himself, Paul 2473, reasoning from an old book, The Logic of Murder — with the faceless state as the true investigating force

Effectively no suspect field: an inverted tale in which the murderer, Paul 2473, is known from the outset; the entire population of Complex 55 (100,000) is treated as an undifferentiated suspect pool, screened en masse rather than individually.

The mass pre-dawn muster and floodlit ordeal reads to Paul (and reader) as a fearsome interrogation, then appears harmlessly to be mere inoculation shots — a plague scare — which lulls him before the truth serum works.

Fair-play clues are planted early: the state's total absence of murder statutes, the surveillance microphones/screens, and pervasive scientific/pharmacological control are all shown to the reader before the chemical interrogation resolves the case.
A truth-serum injection administered to the entire population under cover of a medical screening; under it Paul answers a direct question truthfully and convicts himself.

A totalitarian technocracy: Complex 55, with Platoons, Compatibility Tests, Mating Assignments, work quotas, Caressing Booths, and a hierarchy in which people are 'state property' and treason outranks all crimes.

Paul's alibi is structural rather than verbal: as an air filtration engineer he can rove anywhere, so his presence or absence is never questioned; it is never tested because chemical confession bypasses it.

Inverted: the vulnerability belongs to the murderer — Paul's loneliness and craving for someone to talk to drives the crime, and the case ends by turning Carol, the object of that longing, into his most eager torturer.

Richard 3833 and Laura 6356 have no enemies except Paul 2473, who resents them purely as the assigned mates that separate him from Carol 7427. The grievance is bureaucratic, not personal — Paul barely knows either victim, and Richard greets him amiably about the microscope slide moments before dying.

Complex 55 is a totalitarian dormitory-state of microphones, wall television screens, platoons and assigned cubicles. Paul exploits the two gaps in it: workers isolated at their stations (Richard in his private corner, Laura alone with her machine) and his own job as air filtration engineer, which licenses him to move anywhere unquestioned. The same total control then makes evasion impossible — the entire population can be assembled and injected.

No suspects are developed; the state has no investigative apparatus and never narrows a field. Paul's own vulnerability is his loneliness — the craving for someone to talk to privately — which the crime is meant to remedy and which finally exposes his miscalculation.

The narration is close third-person locked to Paul's reasoning, which is confidently wrong at every turn: he trusts a decayed pre-collapse book's statistics, assumes the state's lack of a murder statute means impunity, assumes the floodlit assembly proves ignorance, and assumes Carol shares his feelings. The reader inherits his misjudgments until the injection and the glass cage overturn them.

Paul's method rests on his physiological training — knowing where to place a sharpened steel blade against the human body — chosen by elimination since he has no gun, no poisons, and is weaker than Richard. The countervailing technical detail is the state's chemistry: a serum that removes the will to lie, against which planning is useless.

Paul kills not from hatred but from a starved human need for intimacy and private speech in a society that has engineered both out of existence; his motive is love and loneliness, and his crime is punished not as a wrong against persons but as destruction of 'valuable state property' — making the regime's public torture arguably more monstrous than the murders.

Murder disguised as a hunting accident: Cozenka shoots her husband at night claiming she mistook him for the escaped 'vicious' leopard Demon. Central question: was the cat actually dangerous, i.e. was the shooting truly a mistake?

Bender's isolated twenty-room lodge and private African animal preserve, twenty miles from a whistle stop in the remote Southwest, with only the three principals, the narrator and a small staff present
Cozenka fired the shot with Peter Wyndham as co-conspirator (he secretly tamed Demon, then shot the cat to destroy the evidence); motive was Bender's money and her love for Wyndham
Ken Bender, clumsy, boring Texas oil millionaire who married Cozenka; killable because his vast fortune passed to a wife who loved another man and only wanted his money

Only partial: Payne reasons that the missing footage of Demon must exist, finds a hidden 16mm reel showing the leopard tamed and purring; the inquest jury calls for further investigation, but the grand jury refuses to indict. Both culprits die within six months (buffalo, car crash) — order restored by chance, not justice
Marty Payne, a magazine writer and houseguest — an outsider witness who becomes amateur accuser; official counterpart Sheriff Henderson and coroner Doctor Wendell

Small closed cast of three principals plus narrator: Cozenka (Eurasian wife, motive: inherited millions and freedom from a bore she never loved, opportunity: fired the shot), Peter Wyndham (her lover/white hunter, motive: her money, opportunity: staged the 'vicious' cat and shot Demon to destroy evidence), Ken Bender (the wealthy husband, victim), and Marty Payne (journalist-witness). Guilt is joint; no genuine alternative suspect exists — the 'suspect' offered to the world is the leopard itself

The black leopard Demon, deliberately presented as savage and treacherous so the shooting would read as a hunting accident; reinforced by Wyndham's staged warning at the cage and by shooting the cat afterward to remove the only living disproof.

Fair-play: the reader sees every clue as Payne does — the couple standing 'very close,' Wyndham's over-emphatic warning, Bender's confided fear, and above all the leopard's tame visit to the den before the shot; the hidden taming film is deduced from the reader-visible absence of Demon from the Africa footage.

Physical demonstration at the coroner's inquest: the concealed sixteen-millimeter reel of Demon's taming, screened with sound track showing Cozenka frolicking with the gentle cat and the animal purring — proving the beast was tame and the 'accident' impossible.

Texas oil money and celebrity glamour: an ungainly self-made millionaire buys an African replica preserve for his exotic wife, who keeps a hired 'guide and companion' on the payroll; local law and grand jury defer to wealth, beauty and the battery of defense attorneys money can buy, while the outsider writer has no standing.

No conventional alibi; instead a shared cover story — 'we were hunting separately, I mistook him for the leopard's green eyes' — an accident claim rather than a whereabouts denial, corroborated by Wyndham's account of tracking and killing the cat.

Payne is a journalist who profits from other people's sensations; the case exploits his guilt at having passively watched, dismissed Bender's plea for help, and possibly courted the story — plus his own susceptibility to Cozenka's beauty and his fear for his career.

Ken Bender is undone by the two people closest to him: his wife Cozenka, who took his oil millions but found him a 'crashing bore' and loved his guide instead, and Peter Wyndham, the handsome 'white hunter' whom Bender complaisantly accepted as his wife's constant companion. The grievance is not hatred but suffocated contempt — he loved her hopelessly, and she resented owing everything to a clumsy, childlike man.

Bender's isolated Texas ranch, twenty miles from a whistle stop, remade into a private African replica stocked with dangerous game. The remoteness means no independent witnesses, the nearest law is a half-hour away in Kenton, and the presence of a 'savage' black leopard supplies a ready-made explanation for a night shooting during a hunt with lights off.

Cozenka's vulnerability is her genuine affection for the leopard Demon — the one sincere feeling in her performance — which forced her to hide the film of the tame cat rather than destroy it, and to protest its screening in a way that betrayed her. Wyndham's is his cultivated self-control: his over-eager warning about the cat's 'treachery' and his desperate haste to shoot Demon read as guilt. Marty Payne himself is wounded by his trade — a magazine writer sensation-hunting, which the sheriff use

Demon, the black leopard — deliberately framed by the culprits as a treacherous killer whose supposed green-eyed charge explains the 'accidental' shot; Wyndham then kills it to destroy the only witness to its tameness.

Marty Payne narrates, and opens by admitting he may have subconsciously let the tragedy happen for the sake of a story; he closes conceding he might have been wrong from the beginning. Cozenka and Wyndham give a coordinated false account of the shooting; Cozenka's grief is explicitly judged by Payne as acting.

Big-cat handling: a jungle cat can in fact be tamed, and Wyndham had secretly done so in Africa, filming the process. The murder method depends on the public belief that leopards are irredeemably vicious — the cat's reputation makes a night 'hunt' with lights off plausible and the mis-aimed shot excusable. Exposure comes from the same knowledge: the cat that visited Payne behaved like a kitten, and the soundtrack records purring, not snarling.

Cozenka is not a simple monster: she genuinely loved the leopard and mourned sacrificing it, and she loved Wyndham as hopelessly as Bender loved her — trapped in the same unreciprocated devotion she inflicted. Payne, meanwhile, admits he would not want to 'pull the switch' on either of them on the evidence he had, and the sheriff's refusal to prosecute is presented as sound legal logic rather than corruption.

Premeditated murder: George Hobday battered on the head while walking across the fields from the station; central question is how Evitt could have done it when a clock and a verified telephone call to the exchange place him at home — i.e. how was the alibi faked?

A small English village community — the Evitts' house, the Hobdays' house down the short lane, the fields between station and house — a tiny circle of neighbours/partners and a fixed Wednesday bridge routine
Harry Evitt, aided by his wife Rina, murdered his partner to prevent exposure of the money he had been stealing from the firm; Rina altered the clock and made a fake phone call to build his alibi
George Hobday, senior partner in the auctioneering firm Hobday and Hobday, killed because he had discovered his partner Harry Evitt's embezzlement and had gone to London to consult an accountant

Inspector Tewson deduces the alibi trick: Rina repeatedly tapped Minnie's watch with a magnetic pencil from the telephone message pad, wrecking the watch so it could not contradict the reset clock and faked exchange call; confronted, Rina breaks and attacks Harry
Detective Inspector Ronald Tewson, official police detective prone to anger at cold-blooded crime, with Sergeant James Geary as sounding board

Small cast: Harry Evitt (partner embezzling from the firm, motive: George discovered the money) and wife Rina as accomplice; Michael Hobday, the nineteen-year-old son, floated as an alternative suspect via a supposed quarrel with his father; Minnie Hobday as witness whose watch is the crux. Reader knows the guilty pair from the opening — an inverted structure where interest lies in whether the timing trick holds.

Rina repeatedly drags Michael into conversation, seeding the idea that the son quarrelled with George; also the 'prowler' suggestion and the notion that Minnie's watch simply went wrong by coincidence.
Fair: the green-and-gold pencil and Rina's habit of tapping Minnie's wrist are shown in the bridge scene long before Tewson interprets them, as is the clock-change plan itself.

Tewson notices the missing pencil belonging to the metal message pad and explains that such pencils contain magnets — repeated tapping on Minnie's watch magnetised and ruined it, destroying the one piece of evidence against the clock; Rina breaks down, confirming it.

English provincial middle-class respectability: a partnership in Hobday and Hobday, auctioneers and estate agents, weekly bridge afternoons, tasteful antique-furnished house bought from magazines; Rina's restless social aspiration and Harry's embezzlement drive the crime.

Harry's alibi: the grandfather clock set back ten minutes plus a faked call to the telephone exchange, so that he appears to be in the room with Minnie when George's six-twenty train arrived and for an hour after.
Tewson's anger at cold-blooded crime: it exhausts him and makes him jump to unwarranted conclusions, the very tendency the Evitts' calculated plot could exploit.

George Hobday's enemy is his own business partner Harry Evitt, who had been embezzling from the firm of Hobday and Hobday and feared discovery; also rumored friction between George and his son Michael, a rumor the Evitts themselves circulated.

A quiet English country house whose weekly ritual bridge party breaks up at exactly six o'clock for the bus — a rigid social timetable Evitt exploits, along with the short cut across the fields from the station and the isolation of the drive where guests are seen off.

Michael Hobday, nineteen, had a 'difficult time' and a reported row with his father, making him look guilty; Minnie's own dazed, grief-broken memory makes her testimony seem self-contradicting and suspicious; Evitt's own nervous feet and compulsive explaining betray him.
Michael Hobday, the nineteen-year-old son, whom Rina repeatedly steers conversation toward, hinting at quarrels with his father.

The Evitts are the liars — both narrate a rehearsed script about the clock and the telephone call. Minnie Hobday is unreliable too, though innocently: grief, sedation and a sabotaged watch make her recant a true statement.

Magnetic disruption of a mechanical watch: memo-pad pencils contain magnets to cling to the metal cover, and repeated tapping against a watch magnetizes the works so it runs wildly fast — destroying it as evidence against a faked clock and phone call.

Evitt is a calculating rather than violent man, driven to murder by the collapse of his embezzlement rather than hatred; he is genuinely terrified and protective of Rina, who is dragged in unwilling and finally breaks under the strain.

Serial murder spree — a killer has shot seven victims (including a five-year-old boy) around Edmonton; the open question is the killer's identity and how he evades a fifty-mile roadblock. The story ends with the eighth killing about to occur inside the car.
A speeding car on an empty flat highway through wheat fields, roads blocked for fifty miles around Edmonton — no house, no tree, only one isolated gas station

The narrator/driver is the actual serial killer, hair dyed brown; he hunted the highway for the copycat attention-seeker, killing out of compulsion and to eliminate the imposter stealing his notoriety
The red-headed hitchhiking kid — a baby-faced runt who deliberately courted publicity by matching the killer's description, making himself the killer's target/rival
No restoration of order — reversal reveal: the reader realizes the driver is the killer and the kid becomes victim number eight
First-person narrator-driver, apparently a neutral motorist, in fact the culprit — an unreliable lens whose calm questioning mimics interrogation

Effectively two figures in a closed car: the red-headed hitchhiker who matches the killer's description and boasts of killing, and the unremarkable brown-haired driver. The kid is built up as the obvious suspect (appearance, manner, obsession with the murders) while the driver is differentiated only by hair color — which turns out to be dyed.

The red-headed kid himself is the planted false trail — his wild talk, his gun fantasies, and his matching description direct suspicion entirely onto him, including from real police who have stopped him three times.

The reader is given every clue the kid has: the narrator's nervous tightness, refusal to phone, avoiding the gas station's radio and phone, his flat 'No' about wondering why the killer did it, and his knowledge of the description. Hair color is the only stated mismatch, and dye is available as an inference.

A single spoken line demonstrating disguise: the kid excludes the driver because of brown hair, and the driver answers that hair can be dyed — retroactively converting every earlier evasion into proof, closed by the count reaching eight.

A rural highway world of wheat fields, isolated gas stations and roadblocks, where status is measured by fear and notoriety — the kid's talk of being 'pushed' by everyone and becoming 'the tallest man in the world' with a gun frames a hierarchy of the small being dominated.
Inverted: the 'investigator' figure is the killer, and the kid's amateur probing exploits his own vanity and compulsion — he is drawn to be recognized and cannot let a poser claim his notoriety.
No web of grievance exists — the victims are strangers chosen at random by a spree killer; the hitchhiker's only 'offense' is resembling the killer and courting the notoriety.

An empty flat prairie highway through wheat fields — no houses, no trees, gas stations forty miles apart and radioless — isolates victim and killer, while roadblocks for fifty miles around Edmonton force the killer to hide in plain sight as an ordinary motorist.
The red-headed kid's wound is his smallness and lifelong sense of being pushed around; he compensates by claiming the killer's glamour, which makes him look guilty to everyone including the police.
The red-headed hitchhiker, picked up by police three times in two days because he fits the broadcast description perfectly and enjoys the fear it produces.

The first-person driver-narrator withholds his own identity as the killer, answering questions flatly and truthfully while concealing everything; the kid in turn lies by implication about being the murderer.
Hair dye as disguise — the manhunt keys entirely on red hair, so altering hair colour defeats the description and lets the killer drive through roadblocks.

The kid's theory — voiced sympathetically — that a man pushed and ordered around all his life finally exploded; the killer neither confirms nor denies it, and shows a flicker of conscience about the five-year-old victim while the boastful kid does not.

A series of poisonings of insect collectors near a New England lake (staged as accidents with their own killing-bottles/snakebite), culminating in the parathion-spray murder of farmer Darrell — the question being whether the deaths were coincidence and who engineered the final killing
A sequestered, superstition-shunned wooded section at the north end of a lake near a small New England farming town where everyone knows everyone, so a stranger is instantly notable

Jim, a frail Lakeville college professor and fanatical insect-avenger, physically commits the killings; but Barbara, the farmer's wife, is the true culprit — she sought him out and manipulated his mania into murdering her husband for money and freedom

Four butterfly/beetle collectors killed as 'executions' for cruelty to insects; ultimately Darrell, the wealthy New England farmer, killable because his wife Barbara wanted his farm and $50,000 insurance to return to Manhattan

Barbara shoots and wounds Jim, telephones Sheriff Reed, plays the grieving widow; Jim is arrested, found sane, convicted and executed in the gas chamber — 'the killing-bottle' — while Barbara goes free and unsuspected
No true detective; the reader alternates between the killer Jim and Barbara, the manipulator-amateur sleuth who deduced the pattern of deaths, while Sheriff Reed is explicitly incompetent

Effectively a two-hander rather than a suspect pool: Jim, the frail entomophile professor who murders butterfly collectors out of righteous zeal, and Barbara, the farmer's wife who manipulates him into killing her wealthy husband Darrell. Sheriff Reed serves as the credulous authority; no other candidates are offered.

The staged framing of the shed killing as a burglary gone wrong ('Darrell thought it was a robber'), plus the earlier deaths dressed as coincidental accidents from killing-bottle fumes and a snakebite.

Reader sees everything the sheriff never does: Barbara's daily month-long stakeout to find the killer, her craving to return to Manhattan 'one way or another', her judo skill, and her coaching Jim on when and where to strike.

Dramatic irony rather than detection: the gas chamber's cyanide fumes mirror the killing-bottle, and Barbara's private accounting of farm plus fifty thousand insurance and a Park Avenue penthouse discloses the true motive to the reader alone.

Rural New England farm country — superstitious locals, a stereotype of grim tight-lipped wealthy farmers, an incurious small-town sheriff — set against a city actress's dependence on her husband's money and her contempt for the life it bought her.
Barbara's alibi is her own performance: she is in the farmhouse, telephones the sheriff, shoots the intruder, and plays the grieving widow — positioning her as victim rather than instigator.
Sheriff Reed's want of imagination and sentimental deference to a grieving widow — the very complaisance Barbara counts on — is the exploited vulnerability.

Darrell, the wealthy New England farmer, is resented by his wife Barbara, who finds marriage to him nauseating monotony and wants Manhattan money and freedom; he is also, as a user of parathion crop spray, an abstract 'killer of millions' in Jim's moral scheme.

The sequestered, 'ghoul-haunted' north-end woods that superstitious locals avoid gives total privacy for meetings and murder; the isolated farm, its pre-dawn storage shed of parathion barrels, and Barbara's insider knowledge of her husband's routine fix exactly when and where the killing can occur.

Jim, the frail entomophile college professor, is a self-confessed 'crackpot' whose obsessive love of insects and prior four killings make him instantly and totally guilty-looking; his loneliness and craving for a kindred spirit is the vulnerability Barbara activates.
None functions as an innocent scapegoat; the intended narrative-level dupe is Jim himself, genuinely guilty of the act but framed as a lone lunatic 'robber' to conceal the true instigator, Barbara.

Barbara's account is wholly false: her professed reverence for 'God's innocent' and her tearful widow's testimony to Sheriff Reed are performance by a former actress; her real aim is insurance money and a Park Avenue penthouse.

Entomological killing-bottle chemistry: potassium cyanide under cotton wool giving almond-scented, instantly lethal fumes; and parathion, an agricultural spray where a few drops on skin kill within minutes — knowledge only a naturalist/farm insider would command.

Jim kills not from hatred but from a coherent, anguished ethic — he sees collectors and sprayers as murderers of innocent life, kills painlessly, and believes he executes justice for creatures no one else defends; Barbara, by contrast, is coldly self-interested, exploiting his sincerity.

Smash-and-grab diamond theft ($58,000) followed by assault on a policeman, and later the shooting murder of the fence Freddy Doyle. Central question: how did the diamonds vanish when the thief was in sight every second and never had them on him?
One city block of Union Street from the Diamond Exchange window to the alleyway, searched exhaustively — only people in physical contact with Hoffman could hold the gems
Peter Arnold, the Diamond Exchange jeweler, in league with Hoffman: he emptied the window himself and staged the robbery for insurance/financial relief, then murdered Doyle to protect himself
Officer Phil Begler, beaten with the cane because he unexpectedly appeared too soon at the scene; and Freddy Doyle, the fence, killed because he had become a liability once the trap exposed the plot

Leopold reasons that Hoffman struck Begler precisely because he did NOT have the diamonds; Arnold's claim of seeing the theft is disproved by the velvet drape blocking his view; Arnold draws his gun, Fletcher wounds him, and the murder weapon is recovered
Captain Leopold of the combined Homicide and Violent Crimes squad, official police detective with Lieutenant Fletcher as sidekick

Small cast: Rudy Hoffman (caught thief, silent), Neil Quart (young 'hero' who tackled him — only person with physical contact, thus prime accomplice suspect), Freddy Doyle (fence, later victim), Glenda (fence's girlfriend/informant), and Peter Arnold (Diamond Exchange owner, financially desperate, the real accomplice)
The 'impossible crime' framing — that the diamonds vanished from Hoffman's person — plus Neil Quart's heroic tackle making him look like the accomplice; in fact the diamonds never left the shop

Fair-play clues given in scene: the opening narration shows Hoffman merely reaching into the window without time to scoop loose stones; the shopkeeper's shouted claim of robbery; the cane not being Hoffman's style; the shooter recognizing Leopold

Leopold's coffee-can trap: hiding the diamonds in the bottom of the can and telling Freddy they were stolen back, which flushes the accomplice into murder; plus the retained murder gun and the drape sightline proving Arnold lied

Urban police-department world: Leopold's Homicide/Violent Crimes squad, loyalty to injured Officer Begler, distrust between street youth and cops, and a respectable jeweler in secret financial ruin exploiting his standing

Neil Quart's alibi for the murder hour — working nights in Bambaum's shipping department — clears him; Arnold's implicit alibi as victim-owner locking up is destroyed by the velvet drape blocking his view
Leopold's pride and personal anger over the beating of fellow officer Begler drives an overreaching trick that gets Freddy Doyle killed, leaving him doubting his own judgment

Freddy Doyle, the murdered fence, was enmeshed with the very conspirators he served: Peter Arnold, the jeweler who needed him to move the diamonds and who shot him when he feared exposure; Hoffman's ring generally; and his own girlfriend Glenda, who betrayed him to the police and whom he threatened to kill.

The busy Union Street corner, constant witness coverage, and immediate police cordon mean Hoffman is in sight every second and the street, alley, boxes and patrol car are all searched — creating a sealed 'impossible crime' zone. Arnold exploited being the insider inside the shop, behind a velvet drape, out of everyone's view.

Neil Quart's vulnerability is his class and appearance — a shaggy-haired young man in paint-stained clothes with contempt for police ("I don't have any love for cops"), so his heroism reads as suspicious and his physical grapple with Hoffman makes him the only possible hand-off point.

Neil Quart, the young man who chased and tackled the robber — hailed as a hero in the morning, hauled in at midnight as the presumed accomplice because he was the only person with physical contact with Hoffman.

Peter Arnold's account is the false frame: as the shop's own man he claims to have watched Hoffman scoop the diamonds from the window while locking up — an impossibility given the velvet drape, and the lie that conceals that he had pocketed the gems himself.

The insider staging of a smash-and-grab: the jeweler empties the display window before closing so the 'thief' takes nothing and can be arrested clean — no loot, no evidence; plus the velvet drape at the window's rear that makes the shopkeeper's claimed sightline impossible. Leopold's own trick — opening a coffee can's bottom with a can opener to hide the pouch and resealing it with a plastic lid — is the mirroring technical touch.

Arnold is a desperate businessman in financial ruin rather than a career criminal; the theft was 'an easy way out,' and the murder came from panic at seeing Leopold, not calculation. Leopold's own culpability is stressed — his clever trick got Freddy Doyle killed and he wrongly hounded an innocent young man.

Death of an outsider on Bald Knob — apparently accidental (crushed by a lightning-split oak) but framed as a supernatural/ritual killing and secret burial; earlier a film director vanished the same way. Question: was this accident, ghost, or murder by the Andersons?
An isolated Ozark hill farm and the taboo Bald Knob above it, near Ozark, Missouri (pop. 800), where outsiders are unwelcome and locals keep their own law

Per the Andersons, the ghost of their hanged Bald Knobber son lured Ed under the oak; effectively Luke and the woman, who deliberately sent him up the hill to protect the hills from outsiders (as with the earlier movie director)
Ed, an arrogant Hollywood location scout who intended to bring a film crew and 'spoil' the hills — an outsider with contempt for locals, hence 'killable' by hill custom
No investigation or justice: the couple bury the body in the hill, evidence washed away by the storm, the folk-ritual chant closing the story
No detective; an omniscient narrator with Ed the doomed outsider as viewpoint — reader learns the truth from the killers themselves

Effectively two living suspects plus a supernatural third: Luke Anderson and his wife ('Ma'), the elderly hill couple with motive (protecting the hills from outsiders and grief over their hanged son) and opportunity; the credited 'killer' is their dead son's ghost/Bald Knobber spirit. A prior victim (the earlier movie director) establishes pattern.

The lightning-split oak presents the death as pure natural accident — reinforced by the storm, the 'rain crow' omen, and the washed-away footprints — misdirecting from the couple's complicity and the pattern of disappeared outsiders.

Fairly seeded: the earlier movie's vanished director, the couple's veiled warnings, the son hanged as a Bald Knobber, the 'spirits never left' legend, and Luke's rain prediction are all given to the reader before the ending.

Confession by casual dialogue at the corpse: the woman's proud statement plus 'where we planted the other man' retroactively converts an accident into serial disposal, sealed by the corn-planting chant.

Ozark hill country insularity versus Hollywood money: vigilante Bald Knobber self-policing replacing absent law, communal loyalty that refused to hang its own, and deep hostility to outsiders who 'spoil' the land.
The couple's implicit alibi is that they stayed at the farmhouse and went to bed during the storm while Ed climbed alone — attributing the death to weather and to their son's spirit.

Ed, a Hollywood location scout, is an outsider whose contempt for the hill people and plan to 'spoil' the land makes enemies of the entire community — chiefly Luke and his wife, who lost their son to outsider-brought law and grief, and who already disposed of a previous movie man the same way.

Remote Ozark hill country: no witnesses, no law nearby, a bald knob shunned by locals, and a spring thunderstorm that erases footprints — the couple exploit local knowledge and terrain to make murder indistinguishable from accident.
Luke and Ma carry the wound of a hanged son and a desecrated Bald Knob; their courtesy masks the grievance the visitor's arrival reactivates.
The vanished son / the Bald Knobber ghost is offered as the 'culprit', deflecting from the living couple who engineered the death.

The wife's folklore narration is the frame: she tells the Bald Knobber legend as history and warning while concealing that she and Luke are steering Ed to his death; her 'it was our son again' attributes to a ghost what her own manipulation accomplished.
Hill-country weather lore: the rain crow foretells a storm, and any hill man knows not to shelter under a tree in a thunderstorm — the ignorance of this makes the method work.
The couple kill to protect land, livelihood and a way of life from developers who 'spoil' the hills, and out of unhealed grief for a son hanged by outsiders' law — defense of home rather than malice.

Murder disguised as suicide: husband gives his wealthy wife a fatal overdose of sleeping pills, staged as the depressive relapse her psychiatrist predicted. Central question is not whodunit but whether the killer will profit.
The intimate domestic/social circle of the Oaks marriage — the bedroom, Dr. Miller's office, Velvet's apartment, and Vossberg the financial manager; a tiny cast of four in a moneyed New York world.

Werther Oaks, the ex-hand-model fortune-hunter husband, killing for Sylvia's inheritance so he can be with his mistress Velvet; he had plotted a car-brake 'accident' for six months before the psychiatrist handed him a safer method.

Sylvia Oaks, a depressed heiress to a $70 million fortune (American Bit & Drill), 'killable' because her documented suicide attempt and psychiatric depression made a staged overdose credible, and her fortune passed to her husband.
Ironic reversal rather than detection: no one exposes Werther, but the happiness he cultivated in Sylvia led her to rewrite her will leaving everything to charity, so he murders for nothing.
No detective; the reader follows the culprit himself, Werther Oaks, with Velvet as secondary viewpoint receiving the news; Dr. Miller functions as unwitting diagnostic 'expert'.

Inverted structure: no suspect pool. Werther Oaks, the fortune-hunting husband, is the known killer from the outset; Velvet (accomplice/mistress), Dr. Miller (unwitting enabler), and Vossberg (financial manager, watchdog) surround him without being suspects.

The staged suicide itself: the psychiatrist's diagnosis of suicidal depression and the earlier 'accidental' overdose are used to make the murder read as self-inflicted — the misdirection is aimed at the world, not the reader.
Fair-play twist clues are planted: Sylvia's stated hatred of her money, her abandonment of luxury on the trip, and her wish to be poor all precede the reveal that she changed her will to charity.
Documentary reveal at the lawyer's office: the altered will demonstrates that Sylvia's induced happiness caused her to give away the entire fortune, voiding the murder's purpose.

Inherited American wealth: an heiress to a seventy-million-dollar industrial fortune (American Bit & Drill), a kept husband on an allowance dispensed by financial manager Vossberg, and the modelling agency economy where women are priced by the hour and downgraded as they age.
No formal alibi; Werther instead builds a psychiatric alibi of motive-absence — the doctor's testimony that Sylvia was suicidal is meant to substitute for concealment of whereabouts.

No investigator; the vulnerability belongs to the murderer — Werther's sentimental conscience and genuine pity for Sylvia, the very decency that compels him to make her happy first, destroys his motive.

Sylvia's antagonists are intimate rather than numerous: her husband Werther, a former hand model married for her fortune and plotting her death with his mistress Velvet; her friends who called Werther a fortune hunter; and Vossberg, the financial manager who controls the purse strings and distrusts Werther.

The gilded constraint of inherited wealth: Werther cannot simply leave, since his allowance is dispensed by Vossberg and everything depends on the will. The psychiatrist's documented suicide diagnosis supplies the social cover, and the moneyless vagabond trip removes them from all supervision — but that same freedom lets Sylvia rewrite her will.

Werther's vulnerability is his vanity and dependence — a kept husband on an allowance, aging (wrinkles on his famous hands), with a mistress whose rates are falling; the marriage's mercenary origin makes him the obvious suspect if suicide is doubted.
Sylvia herself is the manufactured 'culprit' — her documented depression and prior 'accidental' overdose make her own suicide the accepted explanation, deflecting suspicion from Werther entirely.

Werther is the unreliable center: he lies constantly to Sylvia (misreporting Dr. Miller's diagnosis), lies to Vossberg about the Tiffany bracelet, and sincerely believes his own sentimental self-justification that he 'feels sorry' for the woman he intends to murder. Dr. Miller's confident Freudian reading of Sylvia is also a secondhand, self-assured account that Werther weaponizes.

Psychiatric domain knowledge as murder method: a documented clinical diagnosis of unconscious suicidal wish, plus an established prior overdose, makes a fatal dose of sleeping pills medically unremarkable — the psychiatrist becomes the unwitting alibi.

Werther is a murderer who genuinely pities his victim; he postpones the killing for two months at real risk in order to give Sylvia the first happiness of her life, and his tenderness is not entirely counterfeit — the horror is that sincere kindness and premeditated murder coexist in him, and his gift of happiness is what destroys his motive.

Double murder by decapitation: Mrs. Jensen and foreman Carbante beheaded with a lettuce knife in the bedroom of the ranch house. Central question is not who but why — the motive the naive narrator cannot grasp.
Isolated Jensen Produce lettuce ranch outside San Sinandro in the Salinas Valley — bunkhouses, warehouse and big white house, with the owner away and roads later blocked by police
Haysoos, the ugly Mexican picker, drunk on wine — motive is sexual jealousy and humiliation: he lusted after Mrs. Jensen, who favored everyone but him, and Carbante had her
Mrs. Jensen, the beautiful young wife of the elderly owner, who flirted with all the pickers and was sleeping with foreman Carbante; and Carbante, her lover — killed together in bed

Minimal formal resolution: police and ambulance arrive after screams are heard, Haysoos flees through the fields, roads are blockaded and pickers form a posse; the reader — not the narrator — assembles the motive from the planted clues
None in the formal sense — an unreliable, obtuse itinerant fruit-picker narrator who reports every clue while understanding none, forcing the reader into the detective role

Small closed farm cast: Haysoos the sun-blackened Mexican picker who lusts after Mrs. Jensen and resents her preference for Carbante (means: lettuce knife; motive: sexual jealousy/humiliation; opportunity: drunk and alone on payday night); old Mr. Jensen, the cuckolded seventy-year-old owner conveniently 'away on business in Salinas'; Carbante the foreman (victim); and the naive drifter narrator who arrived days earlier and was awake wandering the bunkhouses that night.

The narrator's insistently innocent, admiring voice ('Two of the swellest people you ever wanted to meet') and his emphasis on watching Haysoos drink misdirect from both the absent husband's convenient departure and the narrator's own unaccounted-for movements in the dark.

All physical clues are given plainly to the reader in scene: the razor-sharp lettuce knives every picker carries, Haysoos's repeated 'a man's blood boils' refrain, his heavy drinking and muttering alone, Mrs. Jensen's affair with Carbante, and Mr. Jensen's departure — the mob's conclusion is reached with no evidence the reader hasn't seen.

No formal demonstration — the crime is revealed by the sheeted double stretchers and the pickers' overheard fragments, and the solution is assigned by crowd consensus (decapitation matching a lettuce knife plus Haysoos's absence), with the narrator's uncomprehending closing question inviting the reader to supply the motive.

Rigid agricultural labor hierarchy in the Salinas Valley: absentee elderly Anglo owner, foreman Carbante wielding sexual and employment power, Mexican pickers and seasonal college boys at the bottom, paid in cash per crate; the beautiful young wife circulates as spectacle and Haysoos is the ugly outsider excluded from everything.

Mr. Jensen removes himself with a public, witnessed alibi — announcing to all the pickers he is going to Salinas on business and driving off in the Lincoln; the narrator's only alibi is that he claims he was asleep in his bunk.

The narrator-as-investigator is crippled by naive, worshipful innocence about women and 'nice' people — he cannot process sexuality, jealousy or malice, so Haysoos's plain confessional hints ('a man's blood boils') pass through him uncomprehended, leaving him sick and baffled.

Mrs. Jensen — young wife of the elderly owner — flirted with and slept with many of the workers ('Carbante and a thousand others') while pointedly excluding and humiliating the ugly picker Haysoos; Carbante, the foreman, was her lover and also the boss who told workers to mind their own business. The pickers' reaction ('She had it coming. They both did.') shows a whole camp of resentment.

An isolated Salinas Valley lettuce ranch: workers confined to bunkhouses, the owner away in Salinas for days leaving Carbante in charge and the house free for the lovers, sharp lettuce knives issued as tools, and open fields the killer escapes through while roads are blocked.

Haysoos's wound is sexual humiliation and self-loathing over his ugliness — repeatedly saying 'Haysoos she does not like. Not big ugly Haysoos' and 'a man's blood boils' — which the murder night's drinking activates into rage.

None — the story has no misdirected suspect; guilt is announced flatly at the end. The narrator himself is the only figure the reader might briefly weigh, since he was awake, wandering and watching through windows.

The entire story is told by a naive, semi-literate drifter narrator who cannot read sexual or social meaning: he takes Mrs. Jensen's flirtation as friendliness, misses the college boys' crude jokes, and closes with 'I don't understand it.' The reader sees the adultery, the exclusion and the motive he cannot.

The lettuce-picker's trade: a long, razor-sharp knife used to clip heads close to the ground — the tool and the practiced cutting motion make the double decapitation possible and identify the killer's trade.

Haysoos is not simply a 'crazy' killer: he is a man ground down by ugliness, poverty and exclusion, tormented by a woman who bestowed her favors on everyone but him and by the foreman who possessed her — the pickers themselves judge that the victims 'had it coming.'

Double murder for money in Mexico: a wealthy young woman was killed and burned in a staged car crash so her $50,000 would appear destroyed with her; then her killer's partner Conway was knocked out and rolled off a canyon in his car. Central question: is Conway actually dead?

San Francisco junk-shop/antique district (McAllister Street, the News From Nowhere Emporium) and the isolated, fog-ringed Henderson house at Stinson Beach — a small circuit of places Paulin habitually walks, where only someone who knew Mexico could plant the paintings
Andrew Paulin, the narrator: he and Conway conned and murdered the girl for her $50,000, then Paulin murdered Conway to keep the whole sum for himself

An unattractive, idealistic heiress who wanted to be a patron of the arts and had $50,000 she told her parents was for good works among the Mexican poor — her trust in the two artists made her a target; secondarily Conway, the accomplice, killed to keep all the money

No legal resolution; ironic retribution. The paintings are a trap laid by the surviving Conway, proved when Paulin touches the canvas and finds the paint still wet — he is lured alone into the empty house and a noise announces his killer
Andrew Paulin — the murderer himself as viewpoint 'investigator', reasoning aloud in constant self-directed monologue as he tries to trace who is planting Conway's paintings

Inverted structure: no suspect pool. Paulin is the known killer-protagonist; the only other figures are the presumed-dead Conway (secret survivor and avenger), the murdered heiress, blind old Mac (unwitting or bribed instrument), and the phantom 'Hendersons' who never existed.

The staged provenance story — a touristing couple in their forties named Henderson who bought the paintings in Mexico and moved to Stinson Beach — is a fabricated trail luring Paulin to an empty house; also the pretense that a rival buyer offered fifty dollars.

Fairly seeded: the third painting is done from memory of a pose Paulin never sat for, Conway's body was never found and his car never burned, the paintings appear serially timed to Paulin's route, the Hendersons have no phone, and a fallen sign sits in the weedy lawn — all shown before the wet-paint reveal.

Physical demonstration rather than statement: Paulin's fingers come away from the canvas with wet paint, proving the paintings are newly made and Conway alive — followed by a noise elsewhere in the house.

San Francisco's shabby junk-shop economy of McAllister Street and residential hotels versus Paulin's Russian Hill apartment and sports car funded by stolen money; a patronage relationship underlies the crime — a rich, plain heiress courted as patroness of the arts by two artists.

Not a suspect alibi but its inversion: Conway's supposed death at the bottom of a Mexican canyon functions as his alibi for existence, and the fake accident-crash covers Paulin — the girl believed burned with the $50,000.

Paulin, the de facto investigator of his own trap, is undone by guilty vanity and paranoia — his habit of talking aloud, his compulsion to buy every incriminating canvas, and his refusal to verify Conway's death.

Conway — the painter — was betrayed and murdered by his own partner Paulin, who cheated him out of the $50,000 they had jointly stolen from the girl they murdered together. The grievance web is tight and reciprocal: Conway and Paulin conspired to swindle and kill the heiress, then Paulin eliminated Conway to keep the whole sum. The girl's family and the press are the only outsiders, and they accepted the crash as accident.

The junk-shop district of San Francisco is the trap's mechanism: Paulin's habit of browsing McAllister Street two or three times a week guarantees he will see the window. The final constraint is the isolated Henderson house at Stinson Beach — fog-bound, phoneless, ringed by pines at the end of a road, so no call can be made in advance and no neighbor can hear.

Paulin's vulnerability is his compulsive self-talk — he narrates his guilt aloud in public, moving his lips, and must consciously police the habit. His other wound is greed-driven anxiety: he cannot leave the paintings alone, and each purchase makes him more conspicuous, as the old dealer's teasing about 'some terrific painting' shows.

The 'Hendersons' — the supposed middle-aged tourist couple in their early forties who allegedly brought the paintings back from Mexico and are selling off a dozen more. They are a fiction (or unwitting cover) invented to explain the paintings' provenance and lure Paulin to the beach house.

The entire story is filtered through Paulin's interior monologue — a murderer reassuring himself. His account is unreliable not by lying to the reader but by self-soothing denial: he repeatedly insists Conway is dead while admitting he never verified the body, and he dismisses the paintings as coincidence until the wet paint contradicts him.

Conway's painterly gift — a photographic visual memory allowing him to paint accurate portraits from memory without a sitting, in his 'new neorealism' realist style. This is what makes the fresh paintings possible (Paulin never posed), and the drying time of oil paint is what finally exposes the trap.

Slight and inverted: Paulin's only flicker of conscience is disapproval of Conway's cruelty — objecting that Conway taunted the girl before killing her rather than dispatching her quickly — which he uses to justify murdering Conway. Conway, in turn, is now the avenger, but his revenge repeats the same sadistic toying he was condemned for.

Armed bank robbery followed by kidnapping: a lone gunman robs a small branch bank at closing and takes a teller hostage as cover for his escape. Central question is not whodunit but whether he will escape and what he wants.

The locked branch bank at closing, then the confined interior of the getaway car during a long highway flight across state — a two-person sealed space with roadblocks, toll gates, gas stations and a motel as the only outside contacts

The tall man in the windbreaker, a Korean War veteran trapped in a marriage and life he never chose; he robs the bank not for money but to escape the 'merry-go-round' of providing, leaving the cash to his wife

Marge Elliot, the bank teller — an ordinary suburban wife and mother, 'killable'/takeable simply because she was the last teller on duty at closing time and made a convenient hostage-disguise as a 'wife'

Marge's deliberately abandoned wristwatch in the rest-park outhouse leads police to the car; troopers chase the robber and he goes over a cliff, shot/dead — order 'restored' as Marge returns to Warren, but she weeps for her abductor
Marge, the hostage-victim herself, is the sole point of view — an amateur 'investigator' who both plots escape (leaving clues) and gradually uncovers the robber's motive and her own dissatisfaction

The robber's ordinary appearance and casual notebook-thumbing at the wall desk mislead Marge (and reader) into treating him as a routine customer; later the staged 'married couple quarrelling about split levels' misdirects the state trooper.

The reader sees every escape detail as Marge does: the gun in the pocket, the wig and pink blouse disguise, the second blue car on the parking deck, the abandoned watch in the rest-park outhouse — the watch later proves to be the trace that leads police to him.

Physical trace plus witness memory: the watch Marge deliberately leaves on the outhouse seat, combined with the dog-walking couple recalling the car, demonstrates the trail; the offstage gunfire and 'over the cliff' confirms his predicted end.

Post-war American suburbia: PTA festivals, church committees, subdivisions like 'Pleasant View', split-level houses, breadwinner husbands who merely 'provide' and wives who are perpetually busy — a hierarchy of domestic obligation the robber indicts.

No investigative alibi; instead a fabricated cover identity — the robber passes himself and his hostage off as a bickering married couple on a fishing trip, verified by license and luggage at the toll gate.

Marge, the point-of-view 'investigator' of her captor, is exploited through her own suppressed marital emptiness and lost faith — her longing to be cared for makes her complicit and finally grieving for him.

The closed branch bank at lock-up (no other customers or staff), then the sealed interior of a moving car on a turnpike — toll gates, filling stations and rest parks are the only contact points, each surveilled by the captor so escape is impossible.

The robber's wound is his own life: drafted out of college into Korea, tortured in a prison camp, returned to an automatic marriage and a life of merely 'providing.' Marge's parallel wound is a hollow marriage to Warren and a life of committee busywork.

Told in close third person through Marge, whose perceptions shift from terror to attraction; her own account of her marriage is self-censoring, and the robber answers direct questions ('Do you love her?') evasively.

Prison-camp joint-manipulation technique learned from a Korean guard — wrist pressure that dislocates the shoulder — used silently to control Marge in public; plus disguise craft (blonde wig, changed clothes, switched car) and sedation via sleeping pills dissolved in sweetened coffee.

The robber is gentle, apologetic and protective toward his hostage, robbing not from greed but to escape a suffocating conformist life; he leaves the money to his wife and asks only to state his own terms. Marge, his victim, ends by weeping for him and recoiling from her husband.

Murder disguised as heart failure: film mogul Serge Maillot killed at a press party by high-frequency sound transmitted from the tape recorder to transistors hidden in his hearing-aid battery, which burned his ear. Central question: how was a man killed in plain sight before a crowd and cameras with no apparent weapon?
The L-shaped V.I.P. lounge room at Orly Airport during a champagne press party, sealed off by police; suspects narrowed to the technicians who handled the TV/radio equipment

Demaine, a young fair-haired sound engineer, avenging his father whom Maillot dismissed in 1942 and who died in a camp; he accuses Martine, the widow, of helping by swapping the battery to be rid of her rich old husband

Serge Maillot, 69, 'His Majesty' of French film and theatre — an autocratic producer-director with a young new wife (Martine) who likely married him for money, and a history of dismissing employees, including Demaine's father in 1942

Inspector Jeannot re-stages the death: the gap of silence on the tape plus the melted battery reveal the method; he baits the killer by placing the hearing aid in a colleague's ear, prompting Demaine to break, confess at gunpoint, shoot at Martine, flee and die in an aircraft propeller; Martine is taken in
Adam Venture, a private investigator/oil-business troubleshooter narrating in first person, an outsider gate-crashing the party who works alongside official Inspector Jeannot

A closed pool drawn from the TV/radio technical crew plus the widow: two sound engineers (one fair, nervous — the killer Demaine; one dark-haired), the TV director Riret, the cameraman, and Martine, Maillot's young wife and Venture's former lover, who had motive (money, freedom) and access to the hearing-aid battery. Guests and journalists are dismissed as irrelevant, narrowing suspicion to those who handled the equipment.

The death is staged/read as natural — the sixty-nine-year-old star's collapse diagnosed on the spot as heart failure by his own physician of thirty years; also the suggestion of electrocution from the tested microphone rig, and Burt's assumption that Venture is a hired bodyguard.

All key clues are given to the reader in scene as the narrator perceives them: the concealed hearing-aid wire in the monocle ribbon, the abnormally hot left ear, the melted/fused battery interior, and the inexplicable silent gap on the tape recording — each described before the solution is offered.

A staged re-enactment: Jeannot fits the fatal hearing aid to an innocent dark-haired engineer and replays the tape, provoking the real killer to snatch it away and confess — demonstrating the high-frequency sound weapon (transistor receiver in the battery, sender in the tape recorder) that explains the dead spot on the tape and the heat-melted components.

Parisian celebrity and patronage hierarchy: Serge Maillot, 'His Majesty,' a monarch of theatre and film whose monogram brands everything, surrounded by gossip columnists, critics, UNESCO officials, ministry under-secretaries and dependent employees. Power flows from Maillot's ability to hire and dismiss — his 1942 dismissal of old Demaine, and his marriage to a nightclub dancer, both create the crime.

No conventional alibi work; the murder is remote-triggered so everyone in the room appears equally innocent — the killer stood among the crew in plain view, his 'alibi' being that he never touched the victim. Martine's implication rests on access to the battery, not on whereabouts.

Venture's romantic wound: Martine, the woman he wanted to marry seven months earlier, reappears as Maillot's wife and then his widow and a possible accomplice; his investigation forces him to expose the woman he loved, leaving him empty and unwilling to hear her explanation.

Serge Maillot, the tyrannical 'His Majesty' of Paris theatre and film, had made enemies through his power: the young sound engineer Demaine, whose father Maillot dismissed from his company in 1942 (after which the Germans sent him to a camp where he died); and his much younger wife Martine, a former Boul' Blanche dancer who likely married the 69-year-old for money and wanted him gone. Burt's joke that Maillot needed a bodyguard implies a wider circle of grievance.

Orly Airport, where a delayed Montreal flight strands the detective and a televised press reception is staged in a converted L-shaped lounge. The room's TV/radio apparatus — tape recorder, microphones, spotlights — gives the killer both his instrument and his legitimate presence as a technician; the airport also bounds the suspect pool and finally kills the fleeing culprit on the tarmac in the propellers of the very plane that stranded Venture.

Martine's vulnerability is her past and her marriage: an ex-nightclub dancer who abandoned Venture to marry a rich old man seven months later, she cannot appear innocent of wanting him dead. Her hysterics and sedated silence read as guilt. Venture himself is compromised by his personal history with the widow, which taints his judgment of her.

Martine Maillot, the young widow — the obvious mercenary wife, accused by name by the dying Demaine of swapping the battery, and shot at by him. Her guilt is asserted but never proven; the narrative loads suspicion on her while the actual killer is the inconspicuous fair-haired sound engineer.

Adam Venture narrates as a wry gate-crasher, but he is emotionally entangled: he was in love with Martine and admits jealousy, then judges her guilty on feeling rather than evidence. Demaine's dying accusation against Martine is itself untrustworthy — the raving of a man with a gun — yet Venture accepts it. Martine's own denial is voiceless and drugged.

Murder by high-frequency sound. Demaine replaced the hearing-aid battery with three transistors acting as a receiver, and built a matched transmitter into the tape recorder; switching off the tape and on the sender fired ultrasonic energy above audible range into Maillot's ear. The sound converted to heat, melting the battery and aid, leaving a heated ear, a fused casing, and the tell-tale dead spot on the tape.

Demaine is a son avenging a father: Maillot sacked the elder Demaine in 1942, and the Germans then deported him to a camp where he died. Yet Maillot could not have foreseen that consequence, and the father was a drunkard who probably deserved dismissal — the son sustained his obsession only by refusing to see it. Venture's verdict on him is pity, not condemnation.
The 1944 strangling of Dorothy Paxton, found near Willow Pool; a fifteen-year-old unsolved cold case — who really killed her, since the chief suspect was never convicted?
The small New England town of Stockton, sixty miles from Boston — a fixed set of long-time residents old enough to remember 1944, centered on the library, Willow Pool and Main Street
Bernard 'Bernie' Waterfield, the officious wartime civil defense chief and druggist; motive implied in his character as a predatory man Mrs. De Ware once knew as a suitor
Dorothy 'Dotty' Paxton, the mayor's pretty daughter, courted by many men while her fiancé served overseas — desirability and rival suitors made her a target

Mrs. De Ware's forged 'overdue' library book baits Gifford into openly reopening the case; pressured by the announced interview and 'new evidence,' Waterfield confesses in a suicide note, exonerating Ralph Addison
Allan Gifford, vacationing journalist and detective-fiction writer — an outsider amateur — manipulated by librarian Mrs. De Ware, the true hidden schemer

Small cold-case cast: Ralph Addison, the girl-crazy bachelor last seen with Dorothy Paxton (opportunity, near-conviction, but innocent); Bernie Waterfield, the officious civil defense warden and rejected former suitor (true killer); Dorothy's soldier fiancé brought back from overseas for questioning; plus 'a lot of fellows were after Dotty'

The overdue library book itself — a forged artifact. Mrs. De Ware faked the October 18, 1944 date stamp on a civil defense book from an estate crate, then dangled it as 'new evidence' to bait Gifford into investigating

Fair-play hints are seeded early: her refusal to let Gifford take or examine the book, the book being uncatalogued and kept in a bottom drawer, the conveniently 'faded' red ink, and her over-eager 'delicious part' narration all precede the revelation

Psychological pressure rather than proof: the bluff of 'interesting new evidence' plus a list of interviews panics Waterfield into shooting himself and leaving a written confession; Mrs. De Ware then confesses the forgery over dessert

A small New England town where the mayor's family, the fire chief, the druggist and the librarian are the power network; an unconvicted suspect lives permanently under 'the cloud,' and local pride in the famous case governs who will talk to an outsider

No formal alibi is examined; Gifford's fictional scenario places the civil defense chief at the post office by the library near Willow Pool on the murder day, implicitly placing Waterfield at the scene

Gifford's writer's slump and creative self-doubt — declaring himself 'through with the clue type' and lonely with his family away — is precisely the vulnerability Mrs. De Ware exploits to set him hunting

Dorothy 'Dotty' Paxton, the mayor's pretty daughter, was pursued by many men while her fiancé was overseas — including the girl-crazy bachelor Ralph Addison, last seen with her, and Bernie Waterfield, the officious civil-defense chief who ultimately confessed.

The small town of Stockton — where everyone remembers, gossip travels, and the library, post office and Willow Pool sit at the end of one side street — makes proximity to the murder scene meaningful and makes a stranger's questions instantly public pressure.

Addison's wound was his reputation as a silly, girl-crazy bachelor who had been chasing the victim — enough to leave a lifelong cloud even without conviction. Waterfield's wound was his self-important pride in his civil-defense role, which made Gifford's questions feel like exposure.
Ralph Addison, the near-convicted principal suspect, innocent but shadowed until death.

Mrs. De Ware is the unreliable narrator: kindly librarian who conceals that Ralph Addison was her brother, that she suspected Waterfield from the start, and that the overdue book and its date were fabricated to manipulate Gifford.

Library circulation practice: the earlier librarian Miss Gill stamped the date a book was taken out, not its due date — so the stamp places a borrower at the scene on the murder day; also the aging/faking of red date-stamp ink.
Mrs. De Ware fabricates evidence and manipulates a friend into a false investigation — a deception, yet driven by fifteen years of loving grief for a brother who died under an unlifted cloud.

Apparent poisoning murder: a young writer confesses to putting poison in his best friend's beer. Central question is not who but why — and ultimately whether it was murder at all, or a suicide falsely claimed as murder.
A basement apartment on Garfield Place, Brooklyn, and the tiny social circle around it — Gruber, Perkins, their super, Professor Stonegell, and a mutual girlfriend.

Larry Perkins, who did not kill anyone: Gruber committed suicide and Perkins burned the note, falsely confessing so he could become a famous murderer since he had failed to become a famous writer — a second, chosen suicide.
Al Gruber, a young ex-Army undiscovered writer living on savings and the GI Bill, despairing over his own worthlessness and obsessed with nihilism — 'killable' because he was already suicidal.

Levine reads Gruber's notebooks and interviews the super, professor and girlfriend, then stages a fake reporter (Ricco) who tells Perkins the story is worthless filler — the collapse of Perkins's fame motive makes him break and admit the suicide. Levine lets the confession and trial stand.

Detective Abraham Levine, 53, of Brooklyn's Forty-Third Precinct — an official police detective obsessed with his own mortality, who reads people by stereotype-then-deviation and cares about 'why' rather than 'who'.

Effectively no suspect spread: Perkins self-accuses immediately; the real question is why, not who. Peripheral figures (the super, Professor Stonegell, a female friend) serve as character witnesses on Perkins and Gruber rather than as alternative culprits.
The confessed murder itself is the misdirection — Perkins' confession and 'pompous ass' motive conceal that Gruber committed suicide and Perkins burned the note to stage a famous murder.

Fair-play clues shown to reader as Levine finds them: the super hearing only two shouts and no struggle, Gruber's notebooks on nihilism and death, the joke 'bottle of poison', and Perkins' hidden flicker of emotion.

Psychological trap: Levine stages a fake Daily News reporter (Detective Ricco) who dismisses the murder as unnewsworthy filler, destroying Perkins' fantasy of fame and provoking him to blurt out the suicide truth.

Working-class Brooklyn brownstone bohemia: broke would-be writers on the GI Bill, night courses at Columbia, a landlord-super, and a precinct police hierarchy that prefers a closed case to a true one.
No alibi at issue — the suspect claims presence and guilt rather than absence; the super's timeline of the shouted 'Al! Al!' at noon fixes the moment of death.
Levine, fifty-three, is obsessed with his failing heart and mortality; two young men freely discarding the life he is losing enrages him into letting Perkins go to the chair.

Al Gruber had no real enemies — only his best friend Larry Perkins, with whom he argued constantly and loudly about writers and ideas; the arguments were affectionate rivalry between two failed, depressed writers, overheard by neighbors as shouting matches.

The chopped-up brownstone basement apartment on Garfield Place, with thin walls and a superintendent watching TV nearby, means every sound is a witness — only two shouts of 'Al! Al!' were heard, no struggle, which fits suicide rather than a poisoning quarrel.

Perkins' wound is his craving for fame without talent — Gruber's notebook diagnoses him as wanting to 'be a writer' rather than to write, living on glibness. That vanity makes him confess to a murder he didn't commit, seeking notoriety as a famous murderer.
Larry Perkins himself — the self-accused 'culprit' who is innocent of murder, having planted himself as the killer by confessing and destroying the suicide note.

Perkins' confession is the unreliable account: he claims he poisoned Gruber's beer, but he burned the suicide note and fabricated the murder. His calm politeness masks a hidden emotion Levine cannot read — terror, rage, or pleading.

The poison itself — a bottle Gruber kept as a running gag, taken in beer, leaving a peaceful, relaxed corpse without spasms; that placid death and the absence of struggle are what make suicide indistinguishable from murder except by motive.

Levine knowingly lets an innocent man go to the chair for a suicide, justifying it by his own terror of aging and death: the young men threw away the years he is losing, so he grants Perkins the end he chose.

Serial burglary-murders: a 'cat-killer' cuts window screens of women living alone, shoots them at close range for small cash; then a copycat murder of Elaine Briscoe staged to match the pattern. Central question: who fits the pattern, and can the imitation be distinguished from the original?
A city district of small remodeled apartment buildings with the largest concentration of single women, canvassed by one door-to-door peddler
Kawalik, a tall thin drug-addicted peddler, robbing lone women for drug money; the copycat killer is reporter Keith Briscoe, who murders his wife Elaine to be free for Faye

Violet Hammerman, 38, a solitary secretary living alone (and Dorothy McGannon) — targeted because they lived alone and kept cash at home; ultimately Elaine Briscoe, the wife Keith hates and cannot divorce
